title: Five Daughters, and a Shepherd for After Moses
summary: The five daughters of Zelophehad, whose father died without sons, ask Moses for a share of land so that their father's name will not disappear. God rules in their favor and sets a general law of inheritance. Then God tells Moses to view the land he will not enter, and at Moses' request appoints Joshua as his successor, commissioned by the laying on of hands before Eleazar and the whole congregation.
story: The second census in chapter 26 counted the heirs of the land, clan by clan, and paused to name five women: the daughters of Zelophehad. Now they come forward. Their case is the first of several matters that prepare Israel to live in a land it has not yet entered, and it will be picked up again in chapter 36, which closes the book. The second half of the chapter turns to Moses himself. His exclusion from the land, announced after he struck the rock at Meribah (20:1-13), is about to take effect, and Israel will need a new leader. Joshua, who has served beside Moses since the battle with Amalek (Exodus 17) and who stood with Caleb at Kadesh, is publicly installed. The book of Joshua opens where this chapter points.
historical:
The setting is still the plains of Moab in the fortieth year, with Eleazar now serving as high priest. Zelophehad belonged to the tribe of Manasseh, through Machir and Gilead, a clan that would settle on both sides of the Jordan. The book of Joshua records that the daughters later received their land among their father's brothers, in keeping with this ruling (Joshua 17:3-6). Several of their names also appear as place names in the hill country of Manasseh; Tirzah, for example, later became a capital of the northern kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 15:33), which suggests that the clans descended from these women left a lasting mark on the region.

The mountains of Abarim are the range on the eastern edge of the Jordan valley, overlooking the Dead Sea and Jericho. Deuteronomy identifies the specific peak as Mount Nebo (Deuteronomy 32:49), from which Moses viewed the land before he died (Deuteronomy 34).
cultural:
In ancient Israel, as in most of the ancient Near East, land normally passed from father to son. A man without sons faced the loss of his name, since his property would be absorbed into the holdings of his relatives and his line would vanish from the clan's memory. Mesopotamian legal documents show that daughters could sometimes inherit when there were no sons, but custom varied. The daughters' argument is careful: their father did not die as one of Korah's rebels (whose fate might have been thought to forfeit his claim) but for his own sin, like the rest of his generation. They stand at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, the place of public judgment, and address the whole leadership, which took courage.

The commissioning of Joshua draws on two public customs. The laying on of hands signified the transfer of a role or authority from one person to another, done in the sight of witnesses so no one could later dispute it. The Urim (verse 21), with the Thummim mentioned elsewhere, was a means kept by the high priest for seeking God's decision on specific questions; how exactly it worked is not known. Joshua would not hear God face to face as Moses did, but would receive guidance through the priest.
literary: The chapter has two halves joined by the theme of continuity. Each half begins with someone approaching and making a request, and in each case God answers. The daughters' case follows the form of a legal petition: complaint, argument, a question (“Why should the name of our father disappear from his clan because he had no sons?”), and a request. God's answer affirms them and then generalizes into a law of succession that moves outward in widening circles: son, daughter, brothers, father's brothers, nearest kinsman. Moses' request uses a vivid picture of leadership: a man who will “go out and come in before them”, a phrase for leading in war and daily life, so that the people will not be “like sheep without a shepherd.”

outline.t: The daughters of Zelophehad make their case
God grants their request and sets a law of inheritance
Moses is told to view the land he will not enter
Moses asks God for a shepherd for the people
Joshua is commissioned before Eleazar and the congregation

doctrines.note: The law is not frozen. When a case arises that existing custom did not foresee, Moses brings it before the LORD, and God gives a just ruling that becomes a standing ordinance. Israel's law was meant to secure justice for real families.
God cares that a family's name and place in the land continue. The ruling protects the inheritance of a man with no sons and gives his daughters a secure standing they would not otherwise have had.
Joshua is described as “a man with the Spirit in him.” Leadership among God's people depends first on God's gift, and only then on public recognition and the transfer of authority.

words.note: Nachalah, inheritance. The daughters ask not for money but for an inheritance, a share of the land that would carry their father's name. God says they must be given “property as an inheritance among their father’s brothers”. The word ties their small case to the great promise of land to Abraham's family.

Samakh, to lean on or lay upon. Moses lays his hands on Joshua, a gesture used elsewhere when a worshiper leans his hands on a sacrificial animal and when the Levites were set apart (8:10). It marks identification and transfer. The New Testament church continued the practice in commissioning people for service (Acts 6:6; 1 Timothy 4:14).

Ra'ah, to shepherd or pasture. Moses asks that the people not be like sheep without a shepherd. Across the ancient Near East kings were called shepherds of their people, and in Israel the image stressed care, protection, and guidance. The same verb and picture recur in the prophets' promises of a coming shepherd from David's line (Ezekiel 34:23).

christ: Moses' prayer that Israel not be “like sheep without a shepherd” is echoed in the Gospels. When Jesus saw the crowds, “He had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd” (Mark 6:34; compare Matthew 9:36), and he began to teach and feed them. Jesus calls himself “the good shepherd” who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). The name Joshua (Yehoshua, the LORD saves) is the same name that in Greek becomes Jesus, and Hebrews draws the comparison directly: Joshua led Israel into the land, yet “if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day” (Hebrews 4:8). The connection is a pattern the New Testament itself draws, not a hidden code in the chapter: Joshua leads the people into an earthly inheritance, and Jesus leads his people into the rest that inheritance pointed to.

hard.q: Does this law treat women fairly, if daughters inherit only when there are no sons?
hard.a: The ruling works within a patrilineal system, where land passed through sons, and it does not overturn that system. Daughters inherit only in the absence of sons, and chapter 36 adds that they must marry within their father's tribe. Readers who find this troubling are noticing something real: the law assumes the social order of its time. At the same time, the chapter shows God siding with five women who challenged the custom and saying they “speak correctly.” Their initiative changes the law for all Israel, and they are named in full, three times across the book. Many interpreters see here a principle that pushes beyond its setting: God's concern is to protect the vulnerable within a system and to give standing to those whom custom would leave out. Others emphasize that the law's main purpose is to keep land within the clan, not to address the status of women. Both observations can be true at once.

questions: The daughters of Zelophehad asked for something no one had asked before, and God said they were right. What do you learn from the way they made their case?
Moses asked God for a successor rather than pleading for himself. What does his prayer show about how a leader should think about the people after he is gone?
Joshua was chosen as “a man with the Spirit in him” before he was given authority. What qualities do you look for in those who lead, and what does this passage add?
